result.summary: Ulysses, disguised as a beggar, reaches Eumaeus's hut and is welcomed. He swears Ulysses will return, but Eumaeus disbelieves him, so he tells a false Cretan life story and a tale of a cold night at Troy that wins him a cloak.

scenes.title: Arrival at the swineherd's hut
scenes.summary: Ulysses finds Eumaeus and his yards, is attacked by the dogs, and is rescued and made welcome in the hut.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses could be torn apart by the hounds and must keep his disguise.

scenes.title: Eumaeus laments and doubts
scenes.summary: Eumaeus feeds Ulysses, describes his master's wealth and the suitors' waste, and rejects Ulysses's oath that he will return.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must hide his identity while hearing of the suitors' plunder.

scenes.title: The false Cretan tale
scenes.summary: Ulysses claims to be a Cretan who fought at Troy, was captured in Egypt, betrayed by a Phoenician, shipwrecked, and brought to Ithaca.
scenes.stakes: In the tale, the Cretan faces slavery, shipwreck and death.

scenes.title: Wager and the evening feast
scenes.summary: Eumaeus still disbelieves; they make a wager, then Eumaeus sacrifices a boar and honours the stranger at supper.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses's life is wagered on the truth of his claim.

scenes.title: The cloak story and bedtime
scenes.summary: On a stormy night Ulysses tells of an ambush at Troy where a trick won him a cloak. Eumaeus gives him a bed and goes out to guard the pigs.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses is testing whether he will be left cold; the tale risks nothing.

alias_notes.explanation: Eumaeus is addressed by his occupation.

notable_quotes.reason: Eumaeus states the rule of hospitality: all strangers and beggars are from Jove.
Ulysses says he hates a lying man as he hates hell fire.

analysis.text: Hospitality (xenia) is central: Eumaeus, poor but generous, treats the stranger as under Jove's protection, contrasting with the greedy suitors.
Ulysses's lies, mixing truth and invention, show his cunning and his testing of loyalty.

fun_facts.text: Eumaeus's tale of the borrowed cloak is one of Ulysses's several invented 'Cretan' stories in the poem.

language_notes.text: "Spacious126" contains a stray footnote number (126) from the edition; it is not part of the text. The word simply means roomy.
"Sandals127" likewise carries a footnote marker (127). These were simple footwear cut from a single piece of hide.
"In his own homestead" is ironic emphasis: Ulysses is the true owner of this land, though the dogs and swineherd do not know him.
"Made short work of you" is an idiom meaning would have killed or mauled you quickly.
"Chamois skin" is the hide of a mountain goat-antelope; here a shaggy, soft skin used as bedding.
"To this you answered, O swineherd Eumaeus" is a formal Homeric address to Eumaeus, used when the narrator speaks directly to a character.
Helen's flight or abduction to Troy caused the Trojan War, in which many Greek men died; Eumaeus blames her whole family.
Ilius is Ilium, another name for Troy.
Girdle: a belt or sash tied round the tunic so he could work freely.
Sprinkling barley meal over the meat was a customary act of sacrificial ritual and a sign of Ulysses sharing the meal.
Freebooters are pirates or raiders who plunder for booty.
Swearing by Jove, hospitality and the hearth invokes the gods who protect guests; the hearth is the household's sacred centre.
Telemachus went to Pylos, home of Nestor, to seek news of his father; the suitors plan to ambush him on his return.
Son of Saturn is Jove (Zeus), whose father was Saturn (Cronus).
Concubine: a woman kept as a secondary partner, often a slave; it explains why he is not a legitimate heir.
Proverb-like saying: the leftover straw shows how fine the grain-ear once was; his present ruin reveals his former greatness.
The 'river' is the Nile, called Aegyptus in this translation; the odd 'going down a river' reflects sailing south from Crete toward Egypt.
Clasping the king's knees and kissing them is the standard gesture of a suppliant begging for mercy.
Jove the protector of strangers (Zeus Xenios) punished those who harmed suppliants and guests; this belief runs through the whole Odyssey.
Dodona was an oracle of Jove in northern Greece, where priests interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak.
Clouts: rags or patches of cloth, here Ulysses' beggar's clothing.
"Spirited him away" means snatched him off unseen; the storm winds (harpies in the original) are blamed for his disappearance without trace.
Aetolian: a man from Aetolia, a region of central Greece. He is a fugitive, having killed someone, seeking refuge as a guest.
Dulichium: an island in the Ionian sea near Ithaca, part of Ulysses' own kingdom. The stranger names it as his supposed destination.
"A pretty figure I should cut" is ironic: he means he would look dreadful, having murdered a guest.
"Take toll of him" means take our share of the pig for ourselves.
Burning bristles from the victim's head as first offering was a sacrificial rite, dedicating the animal to the gods before it was killed.
"Equitable" means fair and just in dividing the shares.
Taphians were seafaring islanders, known as raiders and traders, including slave traders. Mesaulius was bought from them.
"A wet quarter": the West wind was a rainy direction in Greece. Ulysses is hoping to prompt Eumaeus to offer a cloak.
"Got up an ambuscade" means set an ambush; the story is told as one that Ulysses lived through, though he is disguised as a beggar.
"Rime" is frost formed as a white coating of ice crystals; "hoar frost" is similar.
"Gave me his ear" means he listened to me attentively.
"Whereon" means "at which point"; the cloak is taken the moment Thoas leaves.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athena) had disguised Ulysses as an old beggar and sent him to Eumaeus, his loyal swineherd, in the previous book.
The suitors are the men courting Penelope who have taken over Ulysses' household and feast daily on his livestock.
Hospitality to strangers was a sacred duty, protected by Jove (the Greek Zeus), so Ulysses invokes him in thanks.
Greeks believed Jove protected strangers and beggars, so mistreating a guest offended the gods.
The suitors are men courting Penelope who have been consuming Ulysses' household in his long absence.
Ulysses is disguised as a beggar, so Eumaeus does not recognize him.
Arceisius was Ulysses' grandfather; "the house of Arceisius" means the family line.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is god of war; Minerva (Athena) also favours warriors, and she is Ulysses' own patron.
Idomeneus was king of Crete and a leading Greek commander at Troy, so naming him makes the Cretan story plausible.
Phoenicians were seafaring traders of the Levant, often portrayed in the Odyssey as clever and untrustworthy, dealing in slaves.
Dulichium is an island near Ithaca, whose men are among Penelope's suitors.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) protected strangers and suppliants, so hospitality was a religious duty.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes), son of Maia, was a god of herdsmen and travellers; the nymphs also protected country places and flocks.
Laertes is Ulysses' aged father, and the mistress is Penelope. Eumaeus bought Mesaulius without consulting them, showing his independence and loyalty.
Menelaus, king of Sparta, was Helen's husband and a leader of the Greeks at Troy. Ulysses' own name in the story is a trick, since the speaker pretends to be someone else.
Agamemnon was the commander of the whole Greek army at Troy, so a request to him for reinforcements sounds plausible.
Ulysses' son is Telemachus, who is away in search of news of his father; Eumaeus does not know the beggar is Ulysses.

literary_notes.text: Eumaeus' unprompted building of sturdy yards, without telling Penelope or Laertes, shows his loyalty, initiative and thrift.
Comparing the hounds to wolves stresses their ferocity and prepares for the danger Ulysses faces.
Eumaeus laments his master as possibly starving far away, while the audience knows that master is standing before him in disguise.
Eumaeus' gratitude for his master's generosity shows him as loyal, humble and hardworking.
We know the silent beggar is Ulysses, so Eumaeus' account of the suitors feeds his hidden anger.
Eumaeus vividly imagines Ulysses' corpse scattered, while the man is alive and sitting before him.
Ulysses' prediction of his return and vengeance hints at the coming slaughter of the suitors.
Ulysses invents a humble, illegitimate but valiant background, a persona that suits his disguise as a beggar.
Drowning men compared to sea-gulls bobbing on the water gives a vivid, pitiful picture of helplessness.
Ulysses reports news of himself to Eumaeus, who does not know he is speaking to him; the audience enjoys the joke.
The beggar says the gods brought him to a good man's door, which is true, though in a way Eumaeus cannot know.
The narrator's direct address, "O swineherd Eumaeus", is a recurring Homeric apostrophe that shows affection for the character.
Eumaeus laments Ulysses as lost while the listener is Ulysses himself, so his sorrow and disbelief carry pointed irony.
Eumaeus's horror at harming a guest shows his strong sense of piety and hospitality.
The squealing of the pigs being driven in gives a vivid sound picture of the farmyard at evening.
Giving the best cut to the stranger shows Eumaeus's generosity, even though he still doubts the man's tale.
Ulysses tests Eumaeus rather than asking outright, showing his habitual cunning and caution even while disguised.
"As crafty as he was valiant" sums up Ulysses' defining traits, with the beggar praising the man he secretly is.
Eumaeus praises the story and promises help from Ulysses' son, unaware that the old man he addresses is Ulysses himself.
Eumaeus's willingness to sleep outdoors with the pigs in harsh weather shows his loyalty and devotion to his absent master's property.
